title: Who gets more roti, two sharing or four sharing?
description: One roti is cut into two equal parts for two children, and another roti of the same size is cut into four equal parts for four children. The pieces are compared to see which share is more, and Keeko's doubt, that one fourth is more because four is bigger than two, is broken.
teaching_notes: One idea: when the same roti is shared equally, more children means a smaller share for each. Watch for students who think the fraction with the bigger bottom number is the bigger share.

source: If one roti is divided equally between two children, how much roti will each child get? If one roti is shared equally among 4 children, how much will one child get? Which is more, 1/2 roti or 1/4 roti?
video_script.why: The child sees that one roti shared by more children gives each child a smaller share, so one half is more than one fourth.
video_script.substitution: Read one half as the share of one child when a roti is shared between two children, and one fourth as the share when it is shared among four.
video_script.anchor: One roti shared equally between two children, and one roti of the same size shared equally among four children
video_script.wrong_answer: one fourth is more because four is bigger than two
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says one fourth is more because four is bigger than two. A fourth piece laid on a half piece covers only part of it, so the bubble is struck.
video_script.payoff_line: One half roti is more than one fourth roti

final_answer.spoken: one half roti is more than one fourth roti

names.{{NAME_3}}: asks how much roti each child gets when a roti is shared
names.{{NAME_4}}: answers how much roti each child gets

never_show: Keeko's claim written as an inequality
maths_rules: 1 roti cut into 2 equal parts: each part is 1/2 roti
1 roti cut into 4 equal parts: each part is 1/4 roti
the same roti shared by more children gives a smaller share, so 1/4 < 1/2
slip: 4 > 2 does not make 1/4 bigger than 1/2; more sharers means a smaller piece
video_script.design: One idea: the same roti shared by more children gives a smaller share. Assumes the child has met halves and fourths of a roti. Wrong idea: a bigger bottom number means a bigger share. The two rotis stay on the board to the end.

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks one fourth is more because four is bigger than two.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>But four children share the same roti, so each child gets a smaller piece.
More children sharing means a smaller share, even though the number four is bigger.
